value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.3.1 and Table 10
variable_description: The kind of dwelling a client was living in, as one of twelve settings ranging from a private residence to an institutional or crisis placement. It is a Commonwealth Home Support Programme field, so the protocols list it among items that "are required and will only present if the client is participating in the Commonwealth Home Support Programme activity", and it is empty for clients of every other funded activity. HOMELESSCODE and HOUSEHOLDCOMPOSITIONCODE sit beside it on the client record and answer different questions: whether the housing is secure, and who else lives there.
value_definition: A short label, held in the curated extract as a three-character code, drawn from the twelve settings in Table 10 of the protocols: boarding house; crisis, emergency or transition; independent living unit; Indigenous community or settlement; institutional setting such as residential aged care or hospital; private residence owned or being purchased by the client or family; private rental; public rental; public shelter; supported accommodation; other; and not stated.
limitation: The column cannot date the arrangement. The client table holds a current row plus superseded versions behind RECORDSEQNBR, so a move between settings is visible only where the provider updated the record, and there is no date attached to the setting itself. It is also not a homelessness measure, even though public shelter and crisis accommodation overlap with one: HOMELESSCODE carries that judgement, and 'not stated' is a common answer here.
rationale: The DSS Metadata Registry names the field 'Client: Accommodation Type, Code' in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution with format X(3), and the Data Exchange Protocols publish both the setting list and the fact that the field only appears for Commonwealth Home Support Programme clients.
evidence_quote: The following items are required and will only present if the client is participating in the Commonwealth Home Support Programme activity:
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's one-line wording and a generic sentence saying no finite value list is published, which is wrong twice over: the protocols publish the list, and nothing told a reader the field is confined to one programme.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 2015 Aged Care Planning Region maps
variable_description: The aged care planning region the client's residential address fell in, on the boundaries used between February 2015 and April 2018. "The Australian Government uses Aged Care Planning Regions to plan aged care services across Australia", so this is the column that places a Data Exchange client inside an aged care supply unit rather than an ABS statistical one. DSS's own address validation and geocoding service tagged it from the recorded address, in the same pass that produced the SA1 to SA4, LGA and federal electorate codes on the row.
value_definition: A planning region code from the 2015 determination, which the department signed in February 2015 and published as a set of whole-state region maps with a correspondence to 2011 Statistical Areas Level 2. The regions nest inside states and territories and do not cross them.
limitation: The value is not comparable with the 2018 column beside it. The determinations were remade in April 2018 on a different SA2 base, so a client who never moved can hold two different region codes across the two columns, and a change between them is a boundary change rather than a move. The column also says nothing about aged care use: most Data Exchange clients are in programmes with no aged care component.
rationale: The DIL says the code is the 2015 Aged Care Planning Region boundary tagged by the DSS IQ Office geocoder. The Department of Health publishes what the regions are, when the 2015 determinations were signed, and the correspondence to 2011 SA2s.
evidence_quote: The Government signed the determinations for the 2015 Aged Care Planning Regions in February 2015. These were replaced by the current 2018 Aged Care Planning Regions in April 2018.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's wording, which names the geocoding service but never says what an aged care planning region is or who determines it, and gave the same generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 2018 Aged Care Planning Region maps
variable_description: The aged care planning region the client's residential address fell in, on the boundaries in force since April 2018. "The Government signed the determinations for the current 2018 Aged Care Planning Regions in April 2018. These replaced the 2015 Aged Care Planning Regions." DSS's address validation and geocoding service tagged it from the recorded address, so it is derived geography rather than anything the client or provider entered, and it is the current-boundary companion to ACPR2015BOUNDARYCODE on the same row.
value_definition: A planning region code from the 2018 determination, built by aggregating whole 2016 Statistical Areas Level 2; the department publishes both the region shapefile and a correspondence from the regions to 2016 SA2s.
limitation: A region is a planning unit, not a service catchment or a market. Providers deliver across region boundaries and clients travel across them, so counting clients by region measures where people live rather than where they were served. The column also cannot be compared with the 2015 column without the department's correspondence, because the two sets were determined on different SA2 vintages.
rationale: The DIL says the code is the 2018 Aged Care Planning Region boundary tagged by the DSS IQ Office geocoder. The Department of Health publishes the determination date, the region maps and the SA2 correspondence that defines the boundaries.
evidence_quote: The Government signed the determinations for the current 2018 Aged Care Planning Regions in April 2018. These replaced the 2015 Aged Care Planning Regions.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's wording about the geocoding service and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both its definition and its limitation, so nothing on the page said what the region is or how it differs from the 2015 column.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Data Exchange: Program activity identifier, ID number'
variable_description: The funded activity a service was delivered under, which the DSS metadata registry defines as "an identifier for a unique program activity record in the Data Exchange". In special_activity this is the key of the reference table itself: one row per activity, with NAME giving its title, PROGRAMID the programme it sits under, and STARTDATE and ENDDATE the window in which providers could select it when creating a case. Joining that table to the attendance, session and assessment tables is what turns a bare number on a service record into the name of the thing DSS funded.
value_definition: A short whole number, one to three digits in the registry's format N[NN], with no internal structure. The activity's name, its parent programme and its availability dates come from the reference table, not from the digits; SOURCESYSTEMCODE records whether the activity row came from FOFMS or an external system.
limitation: An activity is not an organisation and not an outlet. The same activity is delivered by many providers from many outlets, and one provider commonly delivers several, so an activity count is a count of funding lines rather than of services on the ground. Identifiers are also not stable across programme redesigns: a restructured or renamed activity takes a new number, so a break in a series can be an administrative change rather than a change in service delivery.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the ActivityId data element and gives its numeric format in the same curated DEX tables the PLIDA extract is drawn from, and the registry's own table layout shows the activity reference table holding the name, programme and availability dates against this key.
evidence_quote: An identifier for a unique program activity record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL sentence 'This data item is inclusive of all program activities with sessions recorded in the Data Exchange', which describes the table's coverage rather than the column, and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.2
variable_description: A flag for whether age-appropriate development was one of the reasons a client sought assistance, defined in the protocols as "where the client is seeking to improve age-appropriate development". The row it sits on is one combination of reasons, identified by ASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY, and the flags beside it cover the other domains: community, family, money, employment, education, training, material, housing, mental, personal and physical. The attendance table stores only the key, so this reference table is what unpacks that key into the set of needs recorded.
value_definition: A two-state flag, set when age-appropriate development is one of the reasons in the combination the key stands for. The domain names come from the eleven SCORE circumstance domains, which the protocols reuse for reasons for seeking assistance so that presenting need and measured outcome share a vocabulary.
limitation: The flag records what a provider entered as a presenting reason near the start of service, not a developmental assessment and not a diagnosis. The protocols warn that the real reason often only becomes apparent after the client engages. Reporting is optional and confined to organisations in the partnership approach, so an unset flag means 'not recorded' at least as often as it means 'not a reason'.
rationale: The protocols define the eleven reason-for-seeking-assistance categories and name age-appropriate development among them, and the reference table's columns are those categories one per column against a key.
evidence_quote: Age-appropriate development: where the client is seeking to improve age-appropriate development.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Seeking assistance related to Age appropriate development' and gave the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing explained that the column is one flag in a keyed set or where the categories come from.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.2
variable_description: The client's age in completed years on the day the session took place. It is derived rather than reported: the protocols say date of birth "provides a direct means of calculating the client's age", and CONDUCTEDDATE on the same row gives the session date. Because it is recalculated for every attendance, one client's value rises across their own rows, which is what lets the attendance table carry an age profile without joining back to the client record.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.2
value_definition: A whole number of years, not an age band. Where the client's date of birth was estimated rather than known, flagged by BIRTHDATEESTIMATED and usually set to the first day of a year, the age inherits that approximation.
limitation: This is not the age at which a client entered a service, and it is not a person-level attribute. Because one row exists per attendance, an age distribution built straight off this column counts a person once for every session they attended, so it over-represents frequent attenders unless clients are deduplicated first.
rationale: The protocols state that date of birth is held so the client's age can be calculated, and the DSS metadata registry lists AgeAtSession as an attendance-level field beside the session's conducted date, but neither publishes the unit, so the completed-years reading rests on the custodian's own wording.
evidence_quote: A client's date of birth is recorded for two reasons: it forms part of the SLK and provides a direct means of calculating the client's age.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Whole year age of the client at time of session' and the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, with nothing on the derivation or on the double-counting trap.

value_domain: ASCCEG 2016 cultural and ethnic group code
value_source: ABS, Australian Standard Classification of Cultural and Ethnic Groups (ASCCEG)
variable_description: The cultural or ethnic group a client identified with, coded to the ABS cultural and ethnic groups classification. It is one of the expanded cultural and linguistic diversity items in the partnership approach, so it is optional and reported only by organisations that opted in, unlike BIRTHCOUNTRYCODE and MAINLANGUAGECODE which are part of the priority client record. The protocols specify the source list: ancestry "records a client's ancestry if relevant. The list of values is drawn from the Australian Bureau of Statistics Australian Standard Classification of Cultural and Ethnic Groups (ASCCEG), 2016."
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.9
value_definition: A four-digit numeric code in the DEX curated extract, from a classification that groups cultural and ethnic groups under broad geographic-cultural groups and narrow groups. The four-digit level names the specific group; the leading digits give the broader groupings.
limitation: Ancestry is self-identified and is not birthplace, citizenship, language or Indigenous status, all of which sit in their own columns on the same record. The curated table keeps a single code, so a client who reported more than one ancestry cannot be seen to have done so. Because the field is optional partnership-approach data, a missing value carries no information about the client's background.
rationale: The protocols name ASCCEG 2016 as the value list for the ancestry field, and the DSS metadata registry gives AncestryCode a four-digit numeric format in the Client (DEX Curated) distribution, which is the ASCCEG group-level code length.
evidence_quote: Ancestry: records a client's ancestry if relevant. The list of values is drawn from the Australian Bureau of Statistics Australian Standard Classification of Cultural and Ethnic Groups (ASCCEG), 2016.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL sentence and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so the page never named the classification behind the code or said the field is optional partnership-approach data.

value_domain: SCORE assessment method and assessor label
value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 8.1 and Table 18
variable_description: Who made the SCORE rating on this row and whether a validated instrument was used to produce it. The protocols pair those two facts in one field: "the 'Assessed by' field captures whether a validated tool was used, and who made the assessment", giving eight labels that cross SCORE directly against a validated outcomes tool, each by client, practitioner, joint or support person. It qualifies OUTCOMEDOMAINSCORE on the same row, so a rating from a client's self-assessment can be separated from a practitioner's judgement before the two are pooled.
value_definition: One of eight labels, formed from two method values (SCORE directly, validated outcomes tool) crossed with four assessor values (client, practitioner, joint, support person). ASSESSEDBYCODE beside it holds the same distinction as a code.
limitation: The label does not name the instrument. 'Validated outcomes tool' covers everything from the Kessler 10 to a locally adopted scale mapped across through the DSS translation matrix, so two rows carrying it are not measured the same way. The protocols also treat the field as voluntary, so a blank neither implies SCORE was used directly nor that the rating is unreliable.
rationale: The protocols explain what the field captures and list its eight values in the data values table, and the registry already carries those eight labels as this variable's valid values from the same document.
evidence_quote: When reporting SCORE information into the Data Exchange, the 'Assessed by' field captures whether a validated tool was used, and who made the assessment.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Identifies who performed the SCORE assessment, represented by a label', which misses half the field: the labels also record whether a validated instrument was used.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Assessment (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Client outcome assessment: Created date, DDMMYYYY'
variable_description: The day the outcome assessment was keyed into the Data Exchange, which the DSS metadata registry defines as "the date a given client outcome assessment was entered into a system". It is a data-entry date, not a service date: SESSIONCONDUCTEDDATE on the same row is when the session actually happened, and the two can be weeks apart because providers may enter data at any point in the six-month reporting period. Since 18 August 2018 it is also the field DSS uses to order a client's assessments in place of ASSESSMENTTYPE.
value_definition: A date, published by the registry in DDMMYYYY form. The PLIDA column carries the same value as a date or timestamp; only the day is meaningful for ordering assessments.
limitation: The date cannot be used to time the client's progress. Two assessments entered on the same day may describe sessions months apart, and a late data-entry burst before a reporting deadline compresses many assessments into a few dates. For elapsed time between a pre and post SCORE, the session conducted dates are the fields to use.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its DDMMYYYY format in the curated DEX assessment table the PLIDA extract is drawn from, and records on the same page that assessment ordering moved to the created date in August 2018.
evidence_quote: The date a given client outcome assessment was entered into a system, represented by DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing warned that this is an entry date rather than a service date, or that it now drives assessment ordering.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Assessment (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Data Exchange: Client outcome assessment identifier, ID number'
variable_description: The identifier of one SCORE assessment event for one client, grouping the domain ratings recorded together at a single point in service. It sits one level above SCOREID, which identifies each individual domain rating, so an assessment covering three circumstance domains produces one value here and three SCOREIDs. ATTENDANCEID and SESSIONID on the same row tie the assessment back to the session it was recorded against, which is where the protocols say SCOREs are captured.
value_definition: A system-generated whole number of up to 19 digits, in the registry's format N[N(18)], carrying no information about the client, the domain or the date.
limitation: The identifier does not order anything. Assessments are paired into initial and subsequent SCOREs by their created dates rather than by identifier sequence, so a higher number does not mean a later assessment, and comparing two identifiers says nothing about which came first in a client's service.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its numeric format in the curated DEX assessment table, and the table layout shows it sitting between SCOREID and the session identifiers.
evidence_quote: A system-generated identifier for a unique client outcome assessment record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so nothing explained how the identifier relates to SCOREID or why it cannot be used to order assessments.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 8
variable_description: Whether the SCORE rating was taken near the start of service or later on, recorded as Pre or Post. The protocols pair SCOREs this way: an initial rating towards the beginning of service and a subsequent rating at the end, with a further assessment every six months where practical. The DSS metadata registry warns that this field stopped being the primary ordering item on 18 August 2018 and "should only be used to order assessments when two assessments occurring on the same day relate to the same session", so ASSESSMENTCREATEDDATE is what orders assessments now.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Assessment (DEX Curated) distribution
value_definition: Two labels, Pre and Post, with ASSESSMENTTYPECODE holding the same distinction as PRE and POST. In long-running services a client can have several Post rows, because subsequent SCOREs are repeated at intervals rather than recorded once.
limitation: A Post row is not an exit assessment and does not mean service ended. It also cannot be used to sequence a client's assessments after August 2018, so pairing rows on this field alone can put a later rating before an earlier one.
rationale: The protocols describe initial and subsequent SCORE pairing, and the DSS metadata registry publishes the field's definition together with the note limiting its use for ordering.
evidence_quote: NOTE: As of 18/8/2018, this field is no longer the primary item used to determine assessment order and should only be used to order assessments when two assessments occurring on the same day relate to the same session.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording about the pre- or post-service phase, which reads as though the field reliably orders a client's assessments. The custodian's own registry says it does not.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 8
variable_description: The coded form of the SCORE service phase, PRE or POST, matching the ASSESSMENTTYPE label on the same row. It marks whether the rating is the initial SCORE the protocols ask providers to record towards the beginning of service, or a subsequent one recorded at the end or at intervals to track change. Use it with ASSESSMENTCREATEDDATE, which is what actually orders a client's assessments; on its own the code only says which side of a pair a rating belongs to.
value_definition: Two codes, PRE and POST, carrying exactly the information in ASSESSMENTTYPE. Keeping both is a convenience of the curated extract rather than two separate facts.
limitation: The code says nothing about how much time passed between the two sides of a pair, or how many subsequent ratings a client received. Because the protocols allow repeated subsequent SCOREs, a POST row is not necessarily the last word on a client's outcome and a client can have several.
rationale: The protocols set out initial and subsequent SCORE pairing, and the registry already carries PRE and POST as this variable's valid values from the same document. The code column is the coded twin of the label column in the curated DEX assessment table.
evidence_quote: A client Circumstances and Goals SCORE assessment should be recorded at least twice - towards the beginning of service delivery (pre-SCORE) and again towards the end (post-SCORE).
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that the code duplicates the label column or that it does not order assessments.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.3.1 and Table 11
variable_description: The dollar value of the assistance delivered in a session, for the service types that are measured by cost rather than by time or quantity. It is one form of the Commonwealth Home Support Programme's amount-of-assistance item, which the protocols describe as "measured as hours and minutes, quantity, cost and/or type" and which "will only present once the service type is selected in the session". ASSISTANCEMINUTES beside it carries the time form, and FEECHARGEDAMOUNT is a different thing again: what the client paid, not what the service was worth.
value_definition: A dollar figure recorded against a session. Which sessions carry it depends on the service type: DSS's program specific guidance sets, per service type, whether assistance is counted in hours and minutes, in quantity, in cost or as a type.
limitation: The amount is not the cost of delivering the service and not a payment. It is the value of assistance a provider recorded for a session under one programme's reporting rules, so it cannot be summed across programmes as expenditure, and a zero or blank means the service type is measured some other way rather than that nothing was provided.
rationale: The protocols list amount of assistance as a Commonwealth Home Support Programme mandatory session-level item, name cost as one of its forms, and record that the fields appear only once a service type is chosen.
evidence_quote: Amount of assistance provided: measured as hours and minutes, quantity, cost and/or type. These data fields will only present once the service type is selected in the session.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL sentence and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader could not tell that the column is confined to certain service types, nor that it is not the fee the client paid.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.3.1 and Table 11
variable_description: The time taken to deliver a session's service, in minutes, for the service types measured by duration. It is the hours-and-minutes form of the Commonwealth Home Support Programme's amount-of-assistance item, which the protocols say is "measured as hours and minutes, quantity, cost and/or type", so it is populated for some service types and empty for others. Read it against ATTENDANCECOUNT on the attendance side: minutes are recorded for the session, not per attendee, so a group session's minutes are not client-minutes.
value_definition: Whole minutes of service delivery recorded against one session, with hours entered separately in the portal and carried here as a single minute total. It measures delivery time, not the elapsed length of a case.
limitation: The figure cannot be turned into effort per client. One session's minutes cover everyone who attended, so dividing by attendance is an assumption rather than a measurement, and travel, preparation and administration around the session are outside it. Where a service type is counted by cost or quantity instead, a blank here means the wrong measure was asked for, not that no service occurred.
rationale: The protocols list amount of assistance as a session-level mandatory item for the Commonwealth Home Support Programme, name hours and minutes as one of its forms, and tie which form applies to the service type selected.
evidence_quote: Amount of assistance provided: measured as hours and minutes, quantity, cost and/or type.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL sentence and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that the measure varies by service type or that the minutes belong to the session rather than to each attendee.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.2
variable_description: A key standing for the set of secondary reasons a client sought assistance, resolved through the special_ref_assistance_needed table into one flag per reason domain. Secondary reasons can be several at once, so the curated extract stores the combination as a key rather than as a repeating column; PRIMARYASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY on the same attendance row is the main reason. The protocols say these reasons are "recorded at the case level, to allow organisations to reflect that clients go to different activities to address different needs", which is why the same client can carry different combinations across activities.
value_definition: A whole number that indexes the reference table of reason combinations. The meaning is in the joined row: twelve flag columns covering the eleven SCORE circumstance domains, with education and skills training split across the EDUCEMPL and TRAINING columns.
limitation: The key is not a count and not a rank. Two keys cannot be compared numerically, a larger key does not mean more reasons, and nothing in the table says which secondary reason mattered most. Because reporting reasons is optional partnership-approach data, an unpopulated key means the organisation did not report rather than that the client had no secondary need.
rationale: The protocols define primary and secondary reasons for seeking assistance over eleven categories, and the registry shows the attendance table carrying only keys with a reference table holding one flag per category.
evidence_quote: Secondary reasons for seeking assistance: the secondary reasons for seeking assistance, if relevant select another reason from the eleven possible categories.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only that this is a client's secondary reasons 'represented by a key' and gave the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying which table resolves the key or what the reason categories are.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.6 and Table 7
variable_description: Whether the client identified as being of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin, on the five-response standard the protocols take from the AIHW: no; Aboriginal; Torres Strait Islander; both; and not stated or inadequately described. It is part of the priority client record rather than optional partnership-approach data, so it is present for clients across all funded activities. The protocols are explicit about the last category: "Where a client chooses not to disclose their Indigenous status, it is acceptable to record 'Not stated/Inadequately described'."
value_definition: A short alphabetic label, two to ten characters in the registry's AA[A(8)] format, standing for one of the five AIHW Indigenous status responses. The DSS metadata registry names the element 'Client: Indigenous status, Label'.
limitation: A 'no' and a 'not stated' are different answers and must not be pooled: the second is a refusal or a gap in collection, and treating it as non-Indigenous understates identification. The response is self-identified to a service provider at one point in time, so it is not a population estimate and can differ from what the same person reported to the Census or to another agency.
rationale: The protocols set out why the field is collected, say the five options follow AIHW data collection definitions, and list those options in the priority client-level data table.
evidence_quote: Under standard data collection definitions used by the AIHW, five options are available to record a client's Indigenous status.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so the page never listed the five responses or warned against merging 'no' with 'not stated'.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the attendance identifier
variable_description: The number of people the attendance row stands for, which is one for a named client and the group size for an unidentified-client row. DSS explains the mechanism: it adds unidentified client attendances to the attendance table and sets "AttendanceId to the negative of SessionId, and Participation Type to 'GROUP'", and because they are not linked to individual client records their client identifiers are coded zero. This column is what stops a large community event with no registration from looking like a single attendee.
value_definition: A whole number of attendees for the row. The protocols cap unidentified client numbers at 999 per session and require the session figure to be no greater than the number recorded against the case.
limitation: The count cannot be turned into people. Unidentified attendances carry no client record, so the same person attending three sessions of a community activity adds three to the total with nothing to link them, and summing this column across a case counts attendances rather than individuals. It also says nothing about who attended: no demographic data is recorded against an unidentified client.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry documents how unidentified group attendances are represented in the curated attendance table, and the protocols set the counting rules and limits for unidentified clients at case and session level.
evidence_quote: We add unidentified client attendances to the attendance table and set AttendanceId to the negative of SessionId, and Participation Type to 'GROUP'. Further, because unidentified client attendances are not linked to individual client records, ClientId and CaseClientId are coded as 0.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The number of attendees who attended a given session relating to a given attendance record' and gave the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing explained that the count is normally one and only exceeds one for unidentified group rows.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Data Exchange: Attendance identifier, ID number'
variable_description: The identifier of one person's presence at one session, and the row the assessment tables join back to. DSS notes that the application "only generates attendance IDs for individual clients", whether they attend as a client or as a support person, and that rows for unidentified group attendance are inserted afterwards with the identifier set to the negative of the session identifier. A negative value therefore marks a group row with no client behind it, which is the single most useful thing to know before counting attendances.
value_definition: A whole number of up to 19 digits for individually recorded attendances, generated by the Data Exchange. For unidentified group attendances the value is the negative of SESSIONID rather than a generated identifier, and PARTICIPATIONTYPE on the same row reads GROUP.
limitation: The identifier does not stand for a person or for a session. One session produces many attendance rows and one client produces many across their service, so counting distinct values counts episodes of presence. Filtering out the negative values removes group attendance entirely, which understates reach at community events; keeping them mixes rows that have no client record with rows that do.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element, gives its numeric format and documents exactly how unidentified attendances are encoded in the curated attendance table that the PLIDA extract is drawn from.
evidence_quote: The DEX application only generates attendance IDs for individual clients (either attending as a client or support person - Participation Type in ('CLIENT','SUPPORT')).
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and so gave no warning that some identifiers are negative and stand for anonymous groups.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.11 and Table 17
variable_description: How the clients grouped into a case relate to one another: family, couple, cohabitants, peer support group or community event. The protocols say the field exists because "data is reported to better understand the relationship between clients within a case" and that it "should be based on the relationships self-reported by the client and other attendees". It is the field that separates a counselling case covering a couple from a weekly group with unrelated members, which matters because a case is otherwise just a container of sessions.
value_definition: One of five labels. The protocols define each: a family is two or more people, one at least 15, related by blood, marriage, adoption, step or fostering and usually resident together; a couple is two people in a marriage or marriage-like union usually residing together; cohabitants are people in residence together who are not related or in a domestic relationship; a peer support group is a planned and structured service; and a community event is a large-scale, locality-based event where attendees generally do not register.
limitation: The label describes the case, not any pair of people in it, so it cannot be used to build relationships between named clients. It is optional partnership-approach data and self-reported, so a blank is common and a 'family' case does not certify who is related to whom. A community event case is also where unidentified attendance concentrates, so client-level analysis of those cases will be sparse by design.
rationale: The protocols devote a section to the attendance profile, define each of the five values and list them in the partnership approach case-level data table, which is the same list the registry already carries as this variable's valid values.
evidence_quote: Data is reported to better understand the relationship between clients within a case. This should be based on the relationships self-reported by the client and other attendees.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The relationship between clients within a case, represented by a code' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so a reader learned neither the five categories nor the definitions the protocols attach to them.

value_source: ABS, Standard Australian Classification of Countries (SACC)
variable_description: The country a client said they were born in, coded to the ABS country classification. It is one half of the cultural and linguistic diversity pair in the priority client record, with MAINLANGUAGECODE the other half, and the protocols specify the list: "a list of values is based on the Australian Bureau of Statistics Standard Australian Classification of Countries (SACC), 2016". The DSS metadata registry names the element 'Client: Country of birth, SACC 2016 code', so the vintage is fixed at 2016 regardless of when the client record was created.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.7
value_definition: A four-digit numeric code. ABS describes the classification as having "a three-level hierarchical structure that consists of major groups, minor groups and countries", with one-digit major groups, two-digit minor groups and four-digit countries, so the leading digits give the region and the full code gives the country.
limitation: Country of birth is not ancestry, citizenship, language or migration status, each of which has its own column on the client record, and it says nothing about when or whether the client arrived in Australia. Because the codes are fixed to the 2016 classification, countries that have since changed name or status are coded as they stood then, which matters when joining to a later ABS vintage.
rationale: The protocols name SACC 2016 as the value list for country of birth, the DSS metadata registry names the data element as a SACC 2016 code with a four-digit format, and ABS publishes the classification's structure and code lengths.
evidence_quote: A list of values is based on the Australian Bureau of Statistics Standard Australian Classification of Countries (SACC), 2016
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so the page never named the classification, its vintage or its code length.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.2 and Table 7
variable_description: A marker that the client's date of birth was worked out rather than known. The protocols allow it "where a client does not know their date of birth or does not wish to disclose it", and give the working example of a client who thinks they are about 30 in 2019, whose year of birth is entered as 1989 with the estimate flagged. It qualifies BIRTHMONTH, BIRTHYEAR and every age derived from them, including AGEATSESSION on the attendance rows.
value_definition: A tick box in the portal, carried in the curated extract as a two-state flag. Where it is set, the estimated date is conventionally the first day of the year, so the month has no meaning and the year is an approximation.
limitation: The flag does not say how far out the estimate is, and it is not a measure of data quality for the rest of the record. It also does not tell you whether the client refused or genuinely did not know, which are different situations: the first is a privacy choice, the second is common among clients without documents, and neither can be separated here.
rationale: The protocols explain when the indicator is used, give a worked example of the resulting year of birth, and list it as a tick box in the priority client-level data table.
evidence_quote: Where a client does not know their date of birth or does not wish to disclose it, it is acceptable for an estimated date of birth to be used. An estimated date of birth indicator is in the Data Exchange and should be used to flag when this occurs.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said the flag indicates a birth date estimated to the first day of a year and then repeated a generic sentence as both definition and limitation, so nothing said which other columns the flag qualifies.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Client: Date of birth, Month'
variable_description: The month component of the client's date of birth, kept without the day. The Data Exchange collects a full date of birth, which the protocols say "forms part of the SLK and provides a direct means of calculating the client's age", but the curated extract splits it into month and year so that a client can be aged and profiled without a full identifiable date. Where BIRTHDATEESTIMATED is set the month is an artefact of estimating to the start of a year rather than a reported fact.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.2
value_definition: A month number in the registry's format M[M], so one or two digits from 1 to 12.
limitation: The column cannot give an exact age or a birthday. Combined with BIRTHYEAR it fixes age only to within a year, which is why AGEATSESSION is supplied separately, and it is not a usable component for linking to another dataset's date of birth on its own.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its M[M] format in the curated DEX client table, and the protocols explain why date of birth is collected and how the estimated-date indicator interacts with it.
evidence_quote: The client's month of birth.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL phrase and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that the day has been dropped or how the estimated-date flag affects the month.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Client: Date of birth, Year'
variable_description: The year component of the client's date of birth, the coarser half of the split date the curated extract keeps in place of a full one. It is the column that carries most of the age information on the client record, and it is the one the protocols' estimation rule lands on: a client who believes they are about 30 in 2019 is recorded with a year of 1989 and the estimate flagged. Age at a particular service event comes from AGEATSESSION on the attendance rows rather than from this column alone.
value_definition: A four-digit year in the registry's format YYYY.
limitation: A year of birth is not an age. Two clients born in the same year differ by up to a year in age at any session, and where the estimated-date flag is set the year itself is an approximation, sometimes out by several years for clients without documents. It also cannot be combined with the month to recover a date of birth, because the day was deliberately removed.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its YYYY format in the curated DEX client table, and the protocols give the estimation rule that determines the year when a date of birth is not known.
evidence_quote: The client's year of birth.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the DIL phrase and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, with nothing on the estimation rule that produces many of the values.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.4
variable_description: A flag for whether a client was referred onward for help with a caring role, which the protocols define as "support to caring role: the client is referred to help with their caring responsibilities". It belongs to the referral-purpose set, keyed by REFERRALTOKEY and resolved through this reference table, and it is one of two purposes that exist here but not in the reason-for-assistance set beside it, the other being OTHER. That asymmetry is the point: a service can refer a client on for caring support without the client having come in for it.
value_definition: A two-state flag, set when support to a caring role is one of the purposes in the combination the referral key stands for. The referral purposes are the eleven SCORE circumstance domains plus support to caring role and other.
limitation: The flag records that a referral was made, not that the client took it up or that a service followed. It also does not identify the client as a carer: ISCARER and HASCARER on the client record carry that, and a referral can be made for a client who has never described themselves as a carer. Referrals are session-level and optional, with one internal and one external referral allowed per session, so repeated needs appear as separate sessions rather than as a stronger signal here.
rationale: The protocols list the referral purposes and define support to a caring role among them, and the reference table's columns are those purposes, one per column, against a referral key.
evidence_quote: Support to caring role: the clients is referred to help with their caring responsibilities.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Referred for assistance related to support for a caring role' and gave the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing explained the keyed flag structure or the difference between this and the carer flags on the client record.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the attendance identifier
variable_description: The identifier for one client's membership of one case, so a client attached to three cases has three values and each of their attendances carries the one for the case it belongs to. DSS records that where an attendance row stands for unidentified group attendance rather than a named person, "ClientId and CaseClientId are coded as 0", which makes a zero here the marker of an anonymous attendance rather than a missing value. It sits between the case and the attendance, which is what lets a client's sessions be grouped by the case they were delivered under.
value_definition: A system-generated whole number, of the same shape as the other Data Exchange identifiers, with the single reserved value 0 for unidentified group attendance.
limitation: The identifier is not a client and not a case. Counting distinct values counts client-case pairings, so a person who attends two funded activities is counted twice; deduplicating to people needs the client identifier, and deduplicating to services needs the case identifier. A zero must be excluded from either count rather than treated as one more client.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry documents the column in the curated attendance table and states the reserved zero coding for unidentified attendances, though it does not publish a full definition of the element. The protocols supply the surrounding structure: a case attaches one or more client records, and a client attending several activities has a separate case for each.
evidence_quote: because unidentified client attendances are not linked to individual client records, ClientId and CaseClientId are coded as 0.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader had no way to know that zero is a reserved code rather than a missing identifier.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 4.2
variable_description: The day a case stopped being open, left empty while the case is still running. A case is the container the protocols describe as holding "one or more instances of service (known as sessions) received by a client or group of clients that is expected to lead to a distinct outcome", and it can run across several six-month reporting periods, so this is the only column that bounds it. Read with CONDUCTEDDATE on the sessions inside the case, it gives the length of a service relationship rather than of a single visit.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 4.2
value_definition: A date, empty where the case has not ended. It is repeated on every session row of the case in the curated extract rather than held once per case.
limitation: An empty value does not mean the client is still being served. Cases are closed by providers rather than by the system, so a dormant case with no sessions for years can still look open, and a closed case says nothing about whether the client's need was met; EXITREASONCODE is the field that records why a client's relationship with the service ended.
rationale: The protocols define what a case is and note it can operate over multiple reporting periods, which is what makes an end date meaningful, but they publish no case end date field, so the column's meaning is read from the custodian's wording and the surrounding session table rather than from a definition.
evidence_quote: A case can operate over multiple reporting periods, for instance if a client returns to receive the same service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'The date that a case ends. Null where case has not yet ended.' and the generic no-value-list sentence as both its definition and its limitation, so nothing warned that an open case is not evidence of ongoing service.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.2.1
variable_description: The identifier of the case a session or assessment belongs to, where a case is the grouping of related sessions delivered to a client or group under one activity at one outlet. The protocols make the rules for that grouping explicit: a client attending several funded activities has a separate case for each, and the same service delivered from two outlets is two cases. The identifier is set by the provider and may be free text of up to 50 characters, but "if left blank a system generated number is assigned", which is why most values in the curated extract are numeric.
value_definition: An identifier unique within the organisation, which the protocols require to exclude identifying information such as a client's name or Centrelink reference number. Portal users may leave it blank for a generated number; bulk upload and system-to-system reporters must supply one.
limitation: A case is not an episode of care and not a person. It can hold a couple, a family or an unrelated group of up to 1,000 clients, so counting cases counts service containers rather than clients, and one client's continuous service can be split across several cases when they attend more than one activity or outlet. Provider-set identifiers are also only unique within an organisation, so the same value can appear against different organisations.
rationale: The protocols define a case, set the identifier's format and uniqueness rules, state the 1,000-client limit and describe how one client's service is split across cases by activity and outlet.
evidence_quote: Case ID: an alphanumeric code or title that uniquely identifies the case, and which is named in a way that is meaningful to the user.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so nothing said the identifier is only unique within an organisation or that one client's service can span several cases.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Disability (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Data Exchange: Client disability identifier, ID number'
variable_description: The identifier of one reported disability for one client, so a client who reported both a physical and an intellectual disability has two rows and two values. The table is a history rather than a snapshot: DSS states it "will contain records for any disability that has ever been reported", with CURRENTRECORD marking whether the provider still reports it. That makes this identifier the row key for a many-rows-per-client structure, unlike the one-row-per-client columns in special_client.
value_definition: A system-generated whole number of up to 19 digits, in the registry's format N[N(18)], carrying no information about the client or the disability.
limitation: A count of these identifiers is a count of reports, not of people or of conditions. A client can appear with several rows, some of them no longer current, and a client with no row at all has simply not had a disability recorded rather than been assessed as having none: 'None (no disability)' is a value of DISABILITYCODE, and its absence is not the same thing.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its format in the curated DEX client disability table, and the same page describes the table as holding every disability ever reported with a currency flag.
evidence_quote: A system-generated identifier for a unique client disability record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, without saying that the table holds many rows per client including superseded ones.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.4
variable_description: The suburb of the client's residential address, one of the three address parts the protocols require before a client record can be created: "at a minimum, a client's state, suburb and postcode are considered part of the priority requirements and must be recorded to create the client record". It is the text the provider entered, and it is what the DSS geocoder resolved into the SA1 to SA4, LGA, electorate and aged care region codes further along the row. Where a client would not give an address, the protocols direct providers to record the outlet's suburb instead, so some values describe the service rather than the client.
value_definition: A locality name as entered, not a code. CLIENTADDSOURCEVALIDCOD on the same record carries the address quality assessment, which is what says whether the entered text resolved cleanly.
limitation: The suburb is not reliably the client's own. Homeless clients may be recorded at the suburb where they usually spend the night or at the service they approached, and clients at risk of family violence are deliberately recorded at the outlet's suburb, so concentrations around service locations are an artefact of that rule rather than a residential pattern. As free text it also carries spelling and abbreviation variation that the geography codes do not.
rationale: The protocols state that suburb is one of the mandatory address components of the client record, explain the substitutions allowed for homeless clients and for clients with safety concerns, and describe the conversion of the address to statistical geography.
evidence_quote: At a minimum, a client's state, suburb and postcode are considered part of the priority requirements and must be recorded to create the client record.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Client Address: Suburb' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so nothing warned that a substantial group of values are outlet suburbs recorded in place of a client's own.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.4 and Table 7
variable_description: The postcode of the client's residential address, mandatory alongside suburb and state before a client record can be created. The protocols keep the full address out of released data by converting it to statistical geography: "a geography code is recorded in place of the client's address, which de-identifies the record", so postcode is the coarsest address element that survives as entered. It answers a different question from the SA2 and LGA codes beside it, because postal areas cut across statistical and administrative boundaries.
value_definition: A four-digit postcode, limited to four digits in the portal and held in the registry with format NNNN. It is a postal delivery area rather than a statistical region.
limitation: A postcode is not a place a client can be presumed to live in the way an SA2 can be aggregated. Postal areas are drawn for mail delivery, change without notice and include values reserved for post office boxes and large-volume recipients, so they cannot be aggregated to ABS regions without a concordance. As with the suburb, a client who withheld an address may carry the outlet's postcode.
rationale: The protocols make postcode a mandatory element of the client address, cap it at four digits in the data values table and describe the conversion of the address to statistical geography; the DSS metadata registry gives the field's NNNN format.
evidence_quote: This means that a geography code is recorded in place of the client's address, which de-identifies the record.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Client Address: Postcode' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so the page did not distinguish a postal area from the statistical geography sitting beside it.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Address: State or territory, Code'
variable_description: The state or territory of the client's residential address, defined by DSS as "the state or territory of an address, as represented by a code". With suburb and postcode it is the minimum address the protocols require before a client record can exist, so it is the most complete geography column on the client record and the one to use when the finer codes are missing. STE2016BOUNDARYCODE and STE2021BOUNDARYCODE beside it are the geocoder's ABS-coded equivalents, derived from the address rather than entered with it.
value_definition: A short abbreviation of up to three characters, in the registry's format XXX, rather than an ABS numeric state code.
limitation: The state is the address on file, not where a service was delivered: OUTLETSTATE on the outlet record is that, and cross-border service delivery makes the two differ around Albury, Coolangatta and Canberra. As an entered abbreviation it also will not join to ABS state codes without mapping, and a client recorded at an outlet's address for safety reasons carries the outlet's state.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its three-character format in the curated DEX client table, and the protocols make state one of the mandatory address components.
evidence_quote: The state or territory of an address, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Client Address: State' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, without distinguishing the entered abbreviation from the ABS state codes on the same row.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.2
variable_description: A flag for whether poor community participation and networks was among the reasons a client sought assistance, defined in the protocols as "where the client is seeking to change the impact of poor community participation and networks on their independence, participation and wellbeing". It is one column in the keyed set that ASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY resolves to, sitting beside family, housing, money, employment and the rest. Because the same domain names are used for SCORE circumstance ratings, a client flagged here can be followed into an outcome rating on the matching domain.
value_definition: A two-state flag, set when community participation and networks is one of the reasons in the combination the key stands for. The category is one of the eleven SCORE circumstance domains the protocols reuse for presenting need.
limitation: The flag is a provider's record of a presenting reason, not a measure of social isolation. It says nothing about how isolated the client was or whether the service changed that, which is what the SCORE rating on the same domain is for. Reporting is optional and limited to partnership-approach organisations, so cleared flags are dominated by non-reporting rather than by clients without the need.
rationale: The protocols define the eleven reason-for-seeking-assistance categories and word this one directly, and the reference table's columns are those categories, one per column, against a key.
evidence_quote: Community participation and networks: where the client is seeking to change the impact of poor community participation and networks on their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Seeking assistance related to Community participation and networks' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, without explaining the keyed structure or the link to the SCORE domains.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, data element 'Session: Conducted date, DDMMYYYY'
variable_description: The day the session took place, which is the date every counting rule in the Data Exchange turns on. The protocols count a session against a reporting period "if the date of the session fell within the reporting period and at least one client is attached", and a client and a case are counted for a period on the strength of sessions falling inside it, so this column decides which six-month period a service belongs to. It is also the date AGEATSESSION is calculated against, and the service date to compare with ASSESSMENTCREATEDDATE, which is only when the record was keyed in.
description_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 4.4
value_definition: A date, published by the registry in DDMMYYYY form. Sessions can only be recorded inside an open reporting period or its 30-day close-off, so dates outside a period appear only where DSS granted a system re-opening.
limitation: The date does not say how long the service ran or when the client's need arose. A case spanning years is a sequence of these dates rather than a duration, and a gap between them is not evidence of a break in service, because a provider may record several contacts as one session. It is also not a measure of when the data became available: entry can happen weeks later, up to the close-off deadline.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry defines the data element and its DDMMYYYY format in the curated DEX attendance table, and the protocols set out the counting and reporting-period rules that depend on it.
evidence_quote: The date a given session took place, represented by DDMMYYYY.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'The date a given session took place.' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said that this date drives the reporting-period counting rules or how it differs from the record-created dates.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, DEX Curated distributions
variable_description: The moment the record was first written to the Data Exchange, held for every versioned table in the extract rather than for one kind of record. It is an administrative timestamp, not a service fact: on the activity, organisation, outlet and client tables it sits with UPDATEDDATETIME, SYSSTARTTIME, SYSENDTIME, RECORDSEQNBR and CURRENTRECORD, which together make each table a versioned history. Use it to tell when a row entered the system, never to date the thing the row describes.
description_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Disability (DEX Curated) distribution
value_definition: A date and time. In the DEX curated tables it accompanies the system-time columns that bound each version of a row, so the creation stamp of a superseded version and of its replacement differ.
limitation: The timestamp cannot date the event the record is about. A session recorded three weeks after it happened, an activity created long after the programme began, or a client record migrated from another system will all carry a creation time that has no relation to the underlying date, which lives in CONDUCTEDDATE, STARTDATE or the client's own fields.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry shows CreatedDateTime in every curated DEX distribution alongside the system-versioning columns, but its definition is not published, so the timestamp reading rests on the custodian's wording and on the column's company rather than on a definition.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'The date and time that a given activity record was first created' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and appears on tables that are not activities, so a reader could not tell it is a general system-versioning column.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Client_Disability (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the disability code element
variable_description: Whether the row is the version in force or one the Data Exchange has since superseded, coded 1 for current and 0 for historical. Every versioned table in the extract carries it with RECORDSEQNBR, SYSSTARTTIME and SYSENDTIME, and DSS explains how it is set: "a service provider can delete a disability record, in which case CurrentRecord will be 0 and SysEndTime will be populated with the time that the service provider reported the disability was no longer current". Filtering on it is the difference between the state of the world now and everything ever reported.
value_definition: A two-state flag: 1 for the current version of a record, 0 for a superseded or deleted one, with SYSENDTIME populated when the value is 0.
limitation: A 0 does not mean the fact was wrong. It can mean the provider corrected an error, but equally that a circumstance changed or a record was tidied up, and the flag does not distinguish them. Filtering to current rows also does not guarantee one row per subject: DSS warns that a client may have no current disability records or several, so the flag controls currency, not cardinality.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry states the meaning of the two values and the condition that sets 0 in the curated DEX client disability table, and the same versioning columns appear on the activity, organisation, outlet, programme, service type and client tables in this extract.
evidence_quote: A service provider can delete a disability record, in which case CurrentRecord will be 0 and SysEndTime will be populated with the time that the service provider reported the disability was no longer current.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Flag that indicates whether a record is current (1) or historical (0)' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so nothing told a reader what causes a row to become historical or that filtering to current rows still leaves duplicates.

value_source: DSS Metadata Registry, Attendance (DEX Curated) distribution, note on the delivery organisation element
variable_description: The organisation that actually provided the service, which DSS distinguishes from the funded body: delivery organisations are "organisations delivering services directly to clients. These organisations may receive funding directly or through a Funding Recipient (Lead Organisation)." LEADORGID on the same row is the other half of that pair, so where the two differ the service was subcontracted through a consortium or delivery partnership. Join it to special_organisation for the organisation's ABN, and note that a delivery organisation may run several outlets, which OUTLETID identifies separately.
value_definition: A system-generated whole number identifying an organisation record in the Data Exchange. It is not an ABN: ABN_HASH_TRUNC on the organisation table carries the hashed business number for the same organisation.
limitation: The identifier stands for an organisation as registered in the Data Exchange, not for a service or a site. One organisation can hold several identifiers where it registered separately for different programmes, and organisations that merge or re-register break a provider's history in two. Because the lead organisation is often also the delivery organisation, counting distinct values here does not count subcontracting arrangements.
rationale: The DSS metadata registry publishes the note distinguishing delivery organisations from lead organisations against these two fields in the curated DEX tables, and the protocols describe the delivery partnership and handshake arrangements that make the distinction matter.
evidence_quote: Organisations delivering services directly to clients. These organisations may receive funding directly or through a Funding Recipient (Lead Organisation)
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'A system-generated identifier for a unique service provider record in the Data Exchange, represented by a number' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, which conflates the delivering provider with the funded organisation beside it.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.1.8 and Table 7
variable_description: One disability, impairment or condition a client identified with, drawn from the AIHW groupings the protocols use: intellectual or learning, psychiatric, sensory or speech, physical or diverse, none, and not stated. Clients self-identify and "can identify with more than one group", which is why this sits in its own table with a row per report rather than as a column on the client record. DSS adds that the table "will contain records for any disability that has ever been reported", so CURRENTRECORD is what separates what a client reports now from what they once did.
value_definition: A short label held as an alphabetic code of seven to eleven characters in the registry's A(7)[AAAA] format. The protocols define each grouping by underlying condition, impairment, activity limitation and support need, giving examples: dyslexia under intellectual or learning, autism and depression under psychiatric, deafblindness under sensory or speech, and acquired brain injury under physical or diverse.
limitation: The grouping is not a diagnosis and not a severity measure. It is what a client chose to disclose to a service provider, so it undercounts conditions people do not volunteer, and it cannot be compared with a clinical or NDIS classification, which use different categories. 'None' and an absent row are also not the same: the first is a reported answer, the second is silence.
rationale: The protocols set out the AIHW groupings, define each with examples, list the six values in the priority client-level data table and state that clients may identify with more than one; the DSS metadata registry documents the resulting multi-row structure and its currency flag.
evidence_quote: When recording data about disability, impairments or conditions clients should self-identify, and can identify with more than one group, for example physical/diverse and intellectual/learning.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the DIL wording and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so the page neither listed the groupings nor warned that a client can appear several times, including with superseded rows.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 6.3.1 and Table 10
variable_description: Which Department of Veterans' Affairs card the client holds, if any, across four responses: Gold Card, White Card, Orange Card or other, and no DVA entitlement. It is a Commonwealth Home Support Programme field, listed among items that "are required and will only present if the client is participating in the Commonwealth Home Support Programme activity", so a blank almost always means the client is in a different funded activity rather than that they hold no card. Within that programme it is the field that flags a veteran or war widow whose care may be funded through DVA rather than through aged care.
value_definition: One of four labels distinguishing the card types DVA issues, where a Gold Card covers treatment for all conditions, a White Card covers accepted conditions, and the Orange Card category absorbs other entitlements.
limitation: The card is not a service history and not proof of service. It records an entitlement status a client reported to a community care provider, so it will not match DVA's own records for people whose entitlement changed, and it says nothing about which conditions were accepted or what care DVA funded. Card status is also collected for the client, not for a partner who may be covered under the same entitlement.
rationale: The protocols name DVA card status as a Commonwealth Home Support Programme mandatory client field and list the four values in the programme's client-level data table, which is the list the registry already carries as this variable's valid values.
evidence_quote: DVA card status: a client's Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) card status is collected.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Department of Veteran's Affairs card status, represented by a code' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, so nothing told a reader the field exists for one programme and that blanks are structural.

value_source: DSS, The Data Exchange Protocols (Version 13, 1 March 2026), section 7.6 and Table 16

rationale: The Data Exchange Protocols name and define family functioning as one of the eleven reason categories and one of the thirteen referral purposes, and they list personal and family safety separately.
