value_domain: National Disability Advocacy Program session topic
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 5.3.4 and Table 14, National Disability Advocacy Program session level data
variable_description: The advocacy issue a National Disability Advocacy Program session was about, recorded on the session record. The Protocols describe the item as captured at the session level, where "This field allows organisations to select the reason why a client is accessing a service", and make it mandatory only for that program. The published list is of advocacy issues rather than service types: abuse, neglect and violence, discrimination and rights, NDIS access and planning, housing and homelessness, legal access to justice, transport, and about a dozen more. It sits beside SERVICETYPEID, which records what was delivered, while this records what it was about.
value_definition: One label from a closed list of about twenty advocacy issues published in Table 14 of the Protocols. Despite the column name the stored value is the label text, not a number.
limitation: Only one topic is recorded per session, so a session that dealt with a housing problem and a payment problem shows one of them and the other is invisible. The field is collected only for National Disability Advocacy Program activities, so an empty value almost always means a different program rather than an unknown reason, and it must not be read as a diagnosis, a disability type or an outcome.
rationale: The Protocols name the item, place it at session level, restrict it to the National Disability Advocacy Program and publish its full list of values in Table 14.
evidence_quote: Topic: this item is captured at the session level. This field allows organisations to select the reason why a client is accessing a service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated the custodian's line about the reason a client is accessing a service without saying that only one program collects it or what the topics are, and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: education and skills training domain flag
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), section 6.2 reasons for seeking assistance and section 6.4 referrals to other services
variable_description: A marker that education and skills training was one of the domains recorded for a client, set on two different reference tables. On the reasons-for-assistance table it flags the reason category the Protocols define as "Education and skills training: where the client is seeking to engage with education and skills training to improve their independence, participation and wellbeing"; on the referral table it flags a referral made for that purpose. The columns beside it, HOUSING, EMPLOYMENT, MENTAL, MONEY, PERSONAL and the rest, are the other domains from the same list, and several can be set on one row because a client can present with more than one need.
value_definition: A yes-or-no indicator rather than a code, one column per domain on a reference row keyed by ASSISTANCENEEDEDKEY or REFERRALTOKEY. The domain list is the standard set of SCORE circumstance domains used across the Data Exchange.
limitation: The flag records a presenting need or the purpose of a referral, not anything delivered or achieved: a referral flag means a referral was made, not that the client took it up or got help. Reporting the reason is optional and, as the Protocols note, the real reason often only emerges after a client engages, so an unset flag is not evidence that a client had no training need.
rationale: The Protocols define the eleven reason-for-assistance categories and the matching referral purposes, and this column and its neighbours reproduce that list one column per category, including the CARING and OTHER columns that appear only on the referral table.
evidence_quote: Education and skills training: where the client is seeking to engage with education and skills training to improve their independence, participation and wellbeing.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Seeking assistance related to skills training', which did not say it was a flag, did not name the classification behind it and did not mention the second table where it means a referral purpose, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_domain: count of unidentified attendees at a session
value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 9 priority requirements session level data
variable_description: How many people attended a session without a client record being created for them. The Protocols define the item as "the aggregate number of unidentified clients who attended a session" and say it "should be limited to large groups where the collection of client level information is not feasible", which in practice means public events, information sessions and community outreach. These attendances are the only trace those people leave: they have no client row, no demographics and no person identifier, so nothing about them can be linked to the PLIDA spine.
value_definition: A count of people on the session record, defaulting to zero, entered as a number up to 999, and constrained so that it cannot exceed the case-level figure carried in UNIDENTIFIEDCLIENTCASEMAX.
limitation: The number counts attendances at one session, not people: someone who comes to three sessions is counted three times, and the file gives no way to tell repeat attendance from new attendance. It also carries no age, sex, Indigenous status or cultural and linguistic background, so an event's audience cannot be described at all. Any person-level analysis of the Data Exchange silently drops these people while service-level counts keep them, which is the usual source of a mismatch between the two.
rationale: The Protocols define the session-level item, give its purpose, and specify the field as a number with a default of zero and a maximum of 999 that cannot exceed the case-level value.
evidence_quote: Unidentified client attendance: the aggregate number of unidentified clients who attended a session. This should be limited to large groups where the collection of client level information is not feasible.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The number of unidentified clients for the session', which did not explain who these people are, why they are counted this way or that they cannot be linked, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 2.6 and 5.2.2, and Table 8 priority requirements case level data
variable_description: The case-level number of unidentified clients, carried onto the session row as the ceiling that session attendance sits under. The Protocols explain the split: case-level numbers "estimate the total number of unidentified clients who are anticipated to attend services", the session-level number "records how many unidentified clients actually attended that instance of service", and this "prevents double counting". Their worked example is a case with two sessions of 100 unidentified clients each, which means up to 100 distinct people, not 200. Reading it beside UNIDENTIFIEDCLIENTATTENDANCE on the same row is how the two are meant to be used.
value_definition: A count of people attached to the case rather than to the session, entered as a number up to 999, and repeated on every session record belonging to that case.
limitation: It is an expected ceiling rather than a measured headcount, so it cannot be used as a number of clients served, and adding it up across the sessions of a case counts the same group over and over. It also gives no way to tell how many of the unidentified people at different sessions of a case were the same people, so the true number of distinct attendees lies somewhere between the largest single session and this cap.
rationale: The Protocols set out the case and session split for unidentified clients, state that the case figure is an anticipated total, and give the rule that session attendance must be less than or equal to it.
evidence_quote: Unidentified client numbers captured at the case level estimate the total number of unidentified clients who are anticipated to attend services.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only that it was the total number of unidentified clients across sessions in a case, which reads as a headcount rather than a cap, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_source: DSS Data Exchange Protocols (Version 11, March 2024), sections 3.5 outlets, 5.2 priority requirements and 10.3 reporting deadlines
variable_description: When the Data Exchange system last changed this record, not when anything happened to a client. It sits on the reference tables that describe the service system rather than the service itself, including activity, program, service type, organisation, outlet, client and client disability, always beside CREATEDDATETIME and, on the activity table, beside CURRENTRECORD, RECORDSEQNBR, SYSSTARTTIME and SYSENDTIME, which together hold the record's version history. Use it to work out which version of a reference record you are reading, and use the session date for anything about service delivery.
value_definition: A timestamp with both a date and a time of day, written by the source system when the row was amended, rather than a date reported by the funded organisation.
limitation: The timestamp belongs to the row, not to the thing described: an outlet record updated in 2023 is not evidence the outlet changed in 2023, and the sessions already delivered there are unaffected. It also does not say what changed, so a corrected spelling and a genuine change to a program's end date look identical, and a record never amended keeps a stale value that is easily mistaken for evidence of currency.
rationale: The Protocols describe the entities these tables hold, activities, programs, outlets, organisations and clients, and the reporting cycle that governs when data is entered, but they document what organisations report rather than warehouse audit fields. The audit reading is inferred from the column pairing with CREATEDDATETIME and from the version-history columns on the activity table.
evidence_quote: Organisations can enter data at any time within a reporting period, and are encouraged to do so regularly to make best use of the self-service reports and avoid unnecessary backlog or 'crunch' periods.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The date and time that a given activity record was updated', which named the field without warning that it dates the record and not the service, and it repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.
